app.title: Cell Painting Shortcut Audit
app.summary: A person starts from an overview where every assay endpoint is a dot, coloured by its verdict. The verdicts say whether a full image-feature model beats a cell-count-only baseline, with a count for each verdict. Clicking a dot or searching for an endpoint opens its detail: the verdict, a plain-language explanation, ranking accuracy for each model, the statistics behind the verdict and a reliability diagram. They can also look up one compound to see its dose-response readouts and what each model predicted for it. Then they set full-model against baseline accuracy across all endpoints, filter the results table by category and verdict, and download it. Further tabs test whether certified advantages cluster in particular assay families, and estimate the smallest advantage a smaller study could detect.

task.text: Show, for each assay endpoint, whether a rich morphology model really beats a simple cell-count baseline once testing many endpoints and too-thin data are accounted for, so a person can tell which predictions are a shortcut.

data.text: A precomputed table of results with one row per endpoint: the accuracy of each model, the difference between them with its interval and p and q values, calibration scores and a verdict from a fixed set. Alongside it are out-of-fold predictions for each compound and endpoint, readouts for each compound across concentrations, and enrichment and sensitivity tables.
data.item: an assay endpoint (one binary toxicity or bioactivity readout) with its model comparison and verdict

stage.text: comparing a rich model against a shortcut baseline after the models have been fitted, to confirm which advantages hold before reporting

mechanism.text: A dot grid of every endpoint, grouped and coloured by verdict, drives a detail view: clicking a dot selects that endpoint in the search box below, which shows bar charts and a reliability diagram. The other tabs show the same verdicts as a scatter of full-model against baseline accuracy, a results table filtered by verdict and category with CSV export, a lookup by compound, enrichment tables by assay group, and a study planner driven by sliders.

field.text: auditing image-based morphological profiling models against a cell-count baseline in toxicology

workflow.name: check, item by item, whether a rich model beats a simple baseline, and export the verdicts

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: Each endpoint is a dot in a plate-like grid, grouped by verdict (advantage, positive control, no detectable advantage, indeterminate). A legend gives the count for each verdict, and hovering shows the endpoint's change in AUROC.
Clicking a dot, or typing in the endpoint search box, opens the endpoint's verdict marker, a sentence explaining it, and its compound and active counts.

steps.step: compare the full model with the baseline for that item
steps.here: Horizontal bars show the AUROC of the full profile, morphology plus cell count, the cell-count curve and the single cell-count number. An expander lists the AUROC difference, bootstrap interval, z-score, calibrated p, BH q and the smallest detectable effect. A reliability diagram shows whether the predicted probabilities match how often compounds are actually active.

steps.step: look up one item from the other side
steps.here: Choosing a compound shows its hit chips, its cell count, MT and LDH readouts across eight concentrations on a log axis, and a table of recalibrated predictions for each endpoint, filtered by verdict.

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: A scatter plots full-model AUROC against cell-count AUROC for every endpoint, with a diagonal line. Category and verdict pills narrow the results table, which is sorted by q-value.

Choose which baseline counts as certified and how to group endpoints (target family, assay design, cell type) to get enrichment counts, Fisher and assay-level p and q values, and a table of certified counts under other analysis choices.
A 'Download the audit table (CSV)' button saves the full table of verdicts for every endpoint.

distinctive: The baseline is a deliberately strong shortcut model that sees only cell count across the whole dose-response curve. An advantage therefore means information beyond the confound, not beyond a strawman.
Items with too few positive or negative cases (fewer than 15 of either) get an 'indeterminate' verdict and no claim, kept apart from 'no detectable advantage'.

Verdicts use p-values calibrated against a shuffled-label null, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all endpoints that have enough data, and each endpoint also reports the smallest advantage its data could detect.
A positive-control endpoint, defined from the baseline quantity itself, checks that the audit can catch a pure shortcut.
A planner turns the number of compounds and the share that are active into the smallest detectable advantage for a smaller future study (such as one on organ chips).
